affirmation:link:01:child|verb: is one of the child’s names
affirmation:link:01:child|sense: The child is innocence, play, a new beginning and a sacred yes.
affirmation:chain:01#0|sense: The listener says yes to one joy.
affirmation:chain:01#2|verb: is described as the return of the same life
affirmation:chain:01#2|sense: The animals imagine what Zarathustra would say about the eternal return to the same life.
affirmation:chain:02#1|sense: The child is called a sacred yes.
affirmation:chain:02#2|sense: A sacred yes is needed for the play of creation.
agency:link:02:will|verb: creates spirit as the hand of its will
agency:link:02:will|sense: The creating body makes spirit an instrument of its will.
agency:link:04:creation|verb: tests freedom by one’s own law
agency:link:04:creation|sense: Zarathustra asks whether a person can give themselves good and evil and make their will their law.
agency:link:05:recurrence|verb: is counted by the animals among the causes of return
agency:link:05:recurrence|sense: The animals imagine that Zarathustra would count himself among the causes of eternal return.
agency:chain:01#0|verb: creates spirit as the hand of its will
agency:chain:01#0|sense: The creating body makes spirit an instrument of its will.
agency:chain:01#1|verb: is tested by the possibility of becoming one’s own law
agency:chain:01#1|sense: Whether a person can set their own will above themselves as a law is posed only as a question.
agency:chain:01#2|verb: is tested by the creation of good and evil
agency:chain:01#2|sense: Zarathustra asks whether a person can give themselves their own good and evil.
agency:chain:02#0|verb: is presented as a cause of return
agency:chain:02#0|sense: In an imagined speech, Zarathustra counts himself among the causes of return.
agency:chain:02#1|verb: is described as the return of the same life
agency:chain:02#1|sense: The imagined speech names the very same life.
agency:chain:02#2|sense: The imagined speech contains a renewed proclamation of the overman.
attention:link:05:higher-men|verb: is shared with the higher men
attention:link:05:higher-men|sense: Zarathustra and the higher men listen together to the sound of the bell.
attention:chain:02#0|sense: The higher men and Zarathustra listen together to the sound of the bell; this is the shared attention of those already present, not a gathering.
attention:chain:02#1|verb: are faced with the question of affirmation
attention:chain:02#1|sense: Zarathustra puts a conditional question about affirming joy to the higher men and reveals its connection with affirming sorrow.
attention:chain:02#2|verb: connects with the will to eternity
attention:chain:02#2|sense: The affirmation of one joy is linked to the desire for the eternity of all things: joy wants itself and, with itself, sorrow.
becoming:link:04:dance|verb: is likened to the dance of the gods
becoming:link:04:dance|sense: To Zarathustra all becoming appeared as the dance and mischief of the gods.
becoming:link:06:child|verb: transforms the creator into a newborn child
becoming:link:06:child|sense: The creator must will to be the newborn child, the woman giving birth and the pain of birth.
becoming:chain:01#0|sense: Through his own transformations and dying, the creator justifies the transient, of which the best parables should speak.
becoming:chain:01#1|verb: transforms the creator into a newborn
becoming:chain:01#1|sense: The creator becomes a newborn on condition that he also wills to be the woman giving birth and her pain.
becoming:chain:01#2|verb: is likened to a self-rolling wheel
becoming:chain:01#2|sense: The child is a new beginning, play, a self-rolling wheel, a first movement and a sacred yes.
becoming:chain:02#0|verb: is imagined as the returning great year
becoming:chain:02#0|sense: The animals attribute to Zarathustra a teaching of the great year of becoming, which endlessly turns over and runs anew.
becoming:chain:02#1|verb: is linked to the repetition of the same
becoming:chain:02#1|sense: In the animals’ account, every great year and we within it remain the same in great things and small; in their imagined speech the returning knot of causes creates Zarathustra again.
becoming:chain:02#2|sense: In the words imagined by the animals, Zarathustra would return to the same life and proclaim the overman to human beings again.
bestowing-virtue:chain:01#1|verb: reveals the giver’s need for a receiver
bestowing-virtue:chain:01#1|sense: The giver’s solitude and difficulty in receiving are compared with the question of Zarathustra’s soul: giving is a need of the giver, and receiving can be compassion.
bestowing-virtue:chain:01#2|verb: recognizes a lesson about giving from
bestowing-virtue:chain:01#2|sense: Zarathustra learns a lesson from the rejected voluntary beggar’s experience: giving well is harder than taking well, and good giving is an art.
bestowing-virtue:chain:02#0|verb: takes part in the birth of
bestowing-virtue:chain:02#0|sense: The exalted body, through its delight, draws the spirit to become a creator, an evaluator, a lover and a benefactor at the hour of virtue’s birth.
bestowing-virtue:chain:02#2|sense: Zarathustra calls the overman the meaning of the earth and urges his listeners to will that he be so.
bite:link:05:revenge|verb: threatens to draw him into revenge
bite:link:05:revenge|sense: The tarantula’s bite threatens to infect Zarathustra with a thirst for revenge; he seeks protection from it.
bite:link:06:ring|verb: is compared with the ring’s will in joy
bite:link:06:ring|sense: Joy bites itself; the will of the ring struggles within it.
bite:chain:01#0|sense: Zarathustra’s disgust, along with horror, hatred and compassion, speaks in his call to the shepherd to bite off the snake’s head.
bite:chain:01#1|sense: The shepherd bites off and spits out the snake’s head; afterward he appears transformed and enlightened.
bite:chain:01#2|verb: gives way to the transformed one who laughs
bite:chain:01#2|sense: After biting and freeing himself, the shepherd is a shepherd no longer: the transformed one laughs with a laugh that is not human.
bite:chain:02#0|sense: The shepherd’s bite and joy’s self-biting can be compared as images, but here joy bites itself and the shepherd bites the snake.
child:link:01:lion|sense: After the lion, the spirit becomes a child.
child:link:02:memory|sense: Forgetting is one of the child’s names.
child:link:04:affirmation|sense: The sacred yes is named as one of the child’s names.
child:link:07:redemption|verb: receives the task of redeeming the past
child:link:07:redemption|sense: The listeners must make amends to their children for their descent from their fathers and so redeem the past.
child:link:08:laughing-lion|verb: is heralded by the sign of the laughing lion
child:link:08:laughing-lion|sense: Zarathustra recognizes the lion that has come as the sign that his children are near.
child:chain:01#2|sense: A sacred yes is needed for the play of creation, in which the spirit wills its own will.
child:chain:02#0|verb: prompts the creator to complete himself
child:chain:02#0|sense: The children of hope are companions the creator must create; for their sake Zarathustra must complete himself.
circle:chain:01#2|verb: is linked to biting off the monster’s head
circle:chain:01#2|sense: Zarathustra calls biting off and spitting out the head of the monster that choked him his deliverance; the choking is linked to weariness of humankind and the return of even the smallest human being.
circle:chain:02#1|verb: is challenged by a question about
circle:chain:02#1|sense: After the dwarf’s answer about the circle, Zarathustra demands that he not make things too easy and asks whether the moment and all those present return.
counterfactual:link:01:will|verb: confronts the will’s powerlessness before the past
counterfactual:link:01:will|sense: The accomplished “it was” confronts the will with its inability to will backwards.
counterfactual:link:02:revenge|verb: is compared with the will’s hostility to time
counterfactual:link:02:revenge|sense: Revenge is the will’s resistance to time and what has come to pass.
counterfactual:chain:01#0|verb: causes the will’s powerlessness and disgust, which become revenge
counterfactual:chain:01#0|sense: The will cannot turn back time and takes revenge on those who suffer for its powerlessness before what is done.
counterfactual:chain:01#2|verb: is posed as a task for the creative will
counterfactual:chain:01#2|sense: Redemption would mean transforming “it was” through creative willing; whether this is accomplished remains open.
counterfactual:chain:02#0|sense: The will says of the past “thus I willed it” and continues to will it.
counterfactual:chain:02#2|sense: The animals call it Zarathustra’s fate that he must teach eternal recurrence.
courage:link:07:ugliest-man|verb: echoes in the ugliest man’s answer to death
courage:link:07:ugliest-man|sense: Courage’s formula “once more” sounds again in the ugliest man’s acceptance of the life he has lived, for the sake of one day with Zarathustra.
courage:chain:01#2|verb: becomes a subject of dispute and a question about return
courage:chain:01#2|sense: In response to the dwarf’s circle, Zarathustra asks whether the moment draws itself after it and whether all must eternally return.
creation:link:03:will|sense: Willing liberates because willing is creating.
dance:link:01:spirit-of-gravity|verb: accompanies the call to kill the spirit of gravity with laughter
dance:link:01:spirit-of-gravity|sense: The image of a dancing god expresses lightness alongside the call to overcome the spirit of gravity with laughter.
dance:link:04:becoming|verb: likens becoming to the dance of the gods
dance:link:04:becoming|sense: In Zarathustra’s poetic vision all becoming seems the dance and caprice of the gods.
dance:link:05:laughter|sense: The dancer’s virtue and laughing malice are named together as conditions of love for eternity.
dance:link:07:recurrence|verb: is linked by a condition to love of the ring of recurrence
dance:link:07:recurrence|sense: If Zarathustra’s virtue is a dancer’s virtue, how could he not long for eternity and the ring of recurrence?
dance:chain:02#0|sense: The dancer’s virtue and laughing malice stand together as conditions of the refrain.
dance:chain:02#1|verb: is linked by a condition to longing for the ring
dance:chain:02#1|sense: If Zarathustra’s malice laughs, how could he not long for the wedding ring of recurrence?
difference:link:05:overman|verb: links human inequality with love of the overman
difference:link:05:overman|sense: Love of the overman moves Zarathustra to wish human beings many paths into the future and increasing inequality, rather than equality.
difference:chain:01#2|sense: Whoever creates good and evil must first destroy values; life becomes the adversary even of what it has itself created and loves.
fate:link:03:necessity|verb: is linked to necessity through the will
fate:link:03:necessity|sense: Zarathustra calls his will a necessity and a disposition of the soul to which he gives the name of fate.
fate:link:07:affirmation|verb: is imagined by the animals as the dying man’s blessing of himself
fate:link:07:affirmation|sense: The animals place the herald’s eternal lot and his blessing of himself in an imagined speech by the dying Zarathustra.
fate:chain:01#2|verb: raises the question of liberation from revenge
fate:chain:01#2|sense: The redemption of the past is linked to the question whether the will has unlearned the spirit of revenge against time; its resolution has not yet been declared.
fate:chain:02#2|verb: includes a renewed proclamation of the overman
fate:chain:02#2|sense: In the speech imagined by the animals, Zarathustra returns to the same life and again proclaims the overman to human beings.
gateway:chain:01#2|verb: is challenged by a new question about return
gateway:chain:01#2|sense: After the dwarf’s answer about the circle, Zarathustra demands that he not make the task too easy and asks whether all things and both speakers must eternally return.
gateway:chain:02#1|verb: gives way to the vision of the shepherd
gateway:chain:02#1|sense: After the recollection, Zarathustra hears the dog again and sees a shepherd with a snake in his throat.
great-noon:link:01:overman|verb: names the midpoint on the way to the overman
great-noon:link:01:overman|sense: At the great noon, the human being stands between animal and overman and celebrates the way to evening as hope for a new morning.
great-noon:link:02:affirmation|verb: links going under to blessing the crossing
great-noon:link:02:affirmation|sense: At the great noon, the one going under will bless himself for being one who crosses over, and the sun of his knowledge will stand at noon.
great-noon:link:03:going-under|verb: understands going under as crossing over
great-noon:link:03:going-under|sense: At the great noon, the human being celebrates the way to evening as a way to a new morning, and the one going under blesses himself as one who crosses over.
great-noon:link:04:will|verb: links the will to readiness for it
great-noon:link:04:will|sense: Zarathustra asks his will to guard him against small victories and preserve him for a great destiny, so that he may ripen for the great noon.
great-noon:link:06:eternity|verb: is compared with the well of eternity
great-noon:link:06:eternity|sense: In his noonday sleep Zarathustra asks about falling into the well of eternity and calls it a bright, terrible noonday abyss.
great-noon:link:07:recurrence|verb: is proclaimed again in the imagined return
great-noon:link:07:recurrence|sense: The animals imagine that the dying Zarathustra would speak of returning to the same life and proclaiming the great noon anew.
great-noon:chain:01#0|verb: marks the midpoint on the way to
great-noon:chain:01#0|sense: At the great noon, the human being stands between animal and overman and celebrates the way to evening as hope for a new morning.
great-noon:chain:01#1|verb: is proposed as something to create
great-noon:chain:01#1|sense: Zarathustra calls on his listeners to transform themselves into fathers and ancestors of the overman as their best creation.
great-noon:chain:02#1|verb: entails the desire for all to return when joy is affirmed
great-noon:chain:02#1|sense: If a person has said yes to one joy and wished to repeat a happy moment, then, according to the song, they have wished for everything to return, together with sorrow.
identity:link:02:nausea|verb: deepens weariness of the return of the small
identity:link:02:nausea|sense: The eternal return of even the smallest human being becomes for Zarathustra a weariness of all existence.
identity:link:03:animals|verb: receives a conditional formulation in the animals’ speech
identity:link:03:animals|sense: The eagle and the snake imagine how Zarathustra would speak before death of returning to the same life.
identity:link:06:agency|verb: conceives of himself as one of the causes of return
identity:link:06:agency|sense: In the dying speech imagined by the animals, Zarathustra himself is among the causes of eternal return, and the returning knot of causes creates him again.
identity:chain:01#0|sense: In the speech imagined by the animals, Zarathustra eternally returns to the very same life.
identity:chain:01#1|verb: becomes the teacher’s teaching and fate
identity:chain:01#1|sense: The animals call it Zarathustra’s fate to be the teacher of eternal recurrence.
identity:chain:02#0|verb: heightens weariness of the return of the small
identity:chain:02#0|sense: The eternal return of even the smallest becomes a weariness of all existence.
laughter:link:03:bite|sense: After biting off and spitting out the head, the shepherd leaps up transformed and laughs with an inhuman laugh.
laughter:link:06:dance|sense: Laughing malice and the dancer’s virtue stand alongside the wish that what is heavy become light, in a conditional declaration of love for eternity.
laughter:chain:01#1|sense: Zarathustra calls for the spirit of gravity to be killed with laughter, not anger.
laughter:chain:01#2|verb: is opposed to a light dance
laughter:chain:01#2|sense: In the same monologue, the spirit of gravity, through whom all things fall, is opposed to the god who dances through Zarathustra once he has become light.
lion:chain:02#1|verb: accompanies the sign that the children are near
lion:chain:02#1|sense: The lion’s laughter among the doves forms part of the sign at which Zarathustra says that his children are near.
lion:chain:02#2|verb: accompanies ripeness and the call to noon
lion:chain:02#2|sense: The nearness of the children is named together with Zarathustra’s ripening and his own call to the great noon.
memory:link:01:child|verb: is related to the child through forgetting
memory:link:01:child|sense: The child is called forgetting and a new beginning; its relation to memory rests on their difference, without claiming that memory gives forgetting.
memory:link:03:loneliness|verb: is compared with forgetting in solitude
memory:link:03:loneliness|sense: On returning to solitude, Zarathustra recalls his abandonment among human beings and opposes to it the wisdom of forgetting and passing by.
memory:link:04:attention|verb: is awakened by attention to the howling
memory:link:04:attention|sense: Hearing a dog howl, Zarathustra remembers a similar howl from his distant childhood.
memory:link:05:great-noon|verb: precedes the call to noon through reflection on the trial
memory:link:05:great-noon|sense: Remembering the previous day’s events clarifies the trial of compassion, after which Zarathustra turns to his work and calls for noon; memory is not named as the cause of his ripeness.
memory:chain:01#0|verb: is related to the child through forgetting
memory:chain:01#0|sense: The child is called forgetting and a new beginning; its relation to memory passes through the difference between remembering and forgetting.
memory:chain:01#2|sense: A sacred yes is needed for the play of creation.
memory:chain:02#1|sense: After remembering the howl of his childhood, Zarathustra finds himself among rocks and sees the shepherd; no causal link is asserted.
nausea:link:03:self-overcoming|verb: accompanies the demand to overcome the best
nausea:link:03:self-overcoming|sense: There is something disgusting in the best, and the best must yet be overcome; disgust creates wings and powers that sense springs.
nausea:link:06:fool|verb: rejects the fool’s contempt and passes by
nausea:link:06:fool|sense: Zarathustra rejects the fool’s vengeful manner and, feeling disgust for the city too, advises leaving where love is impossible.
nausea:chain:02#1|verb: brings back even the smallest human being as a trial
nausea:chain:02#1|sense: The eternal return of even the smallest human being constitutes Zarathustra’s disgust with all existence.
nausea:chain:02#2|verb: is accompanied by the animals’ call for a new song
nausea:chain:02#2|sense: After his cry of disgust and recollection of his illness, the animals call on Zarathustra to heal his soul with new songs; he has already found comfort himself in the need to sing again.
necessity:link:04:creation|verb: makes suffering and transformation conditions of the creator’s existence
necessity:link:04:creation|sense: For there to be a creator, suffering and many transformations are necessary; creation, in turn, liberates from suffering.
necessity:link:06:present|verb: links freedom with time that mocks moments
necessity:link:06:present|sense: In a poetic vision all time seems a blessed mockery of moments, and necessity seems freedom itself, playing with the sting of freedom.
necessity:chain:01#2|sense: The animals call it Zarathustra’s fate to be the teacher of eternal recurrence and link that fate to danger and illness.
necessity:chain:02#0|verb: makes suffering and transformation conditions of the creator’s existence
necessity:chain:02#0|sense: For there to be a creator, suffering and many transformations are necessary; creation liberates from suffering.
necessity:chain:02#1|verb: becomes a newborn on condition of birth pangs
necessity:chain:02#1|sense: For the creator himself to become a newborn, he must also will to be the woman giving birth and her pain.
overman:link:01:earth|sense: Zarathustra calls the overman the meaning of the earth and urges his listeners to will this meaning.
overman:link:02:rope-bridge|verb: forms one end of the rope
overman:link:02:rope-bridge|sense: The human being is like a rope between animal and overman; the overman is not identified with the rope.
overman:link:03:creation|sense: The listeners are invited to regard their possible transformation into fathers and ancestors of the overman as their best creation.
overman:link:04:last-man|verb: is relinquished by the crowd in favor of the last man
overman:link:04:last-man|sense: The joyful crowd prefers the last man to the proclaimed overman.
overman:link:05:great-noon|verb: marks the horizon of the great noon’s path
overman:link:05:great-noon|sense: At the great noon, the human being stands halfway between animal and overman and celebrates the way to sunset as a way to a new morning.
overman:link:06:death-of-god|verb: becomes an object of will after the death of God
overman:link:06:death-of-god|sense: After God’s death, the higher men are called upon to will that the overman live.
overman:chain:02#2|sense: In the return of the same life, the word of the great noon of earth and humanity is spoken again.
present:link:04:great-noon|verb: becomes a feature of noonday happiness
present:link:04:great-noon|sense: In the scene of noonday rest, the moment joins the small things that make up the image of the best happiness.
present:chain:02#0|sense: If a person has wished to repeat a moment of happiness, then, according to the song, they have wished for everything to return, including pain.
present:chain:02#2|sense: Joy wants itself, recurrence and the eternity of all things.
recurrence:link:02:fate|sense: The animals call it Zarathustra’s fate that he must be the first to teach eternal recurrence, and link this fate to the greatest danger.
recurrence:link:05:circle|verb: challenges the easy answer of the circle
recurrence:link:05:circle|sense: The dwarf’s answer “time is a circle” prompts Zarathustra’s objection and questions about the eternal repetition of the moment itself and the things connected to it.
recurrence:link:07:affirmation|verb: links one yes to the desire for everything
recurrence:link:07:affirmation|sense: If a person has once wished for one joy to recur, then, through the interconnectedness of things, they have, according to Zarathustra’s song, wished for everything to return, including grief.
recurrence:chain:01#1|verb: answers choking disgust with a bite
recurrence:chain:01#1|sense: Zarathustra links his choking weariness of humankind to the monster whose head he bit off and spat out.
recurrence:chain:01#2|verb: is accompanied by transformation and laughter
recurrence:chain:01#2|sense: The shepherd bites off and spits out the snake’s head, then leaps up transformed and laughs.
recurrence:chain:02#0|sense: Zarathustra asks his listeners whether they have ever said yes to even one joy.
recurrence:chain:02#1|verb: links the desire for one joy to the return of all
recurrence:chain:02#1|sense: If the listeners have wished for one joy twice, then, according to the song, they have wished for everything to return, including grief.
ring:link:02:eternity|verb: expresses longing for union with eternity
ring:link:02:eternity|sense: The wedding ring of recurrence expresses Zarathustra’s passionate longing for his beloved eternity.
ring:link:05:bite|sense: In the song, joy wants itself and bites itself, while the will of the ring struggles within it.
ring:link:06:becoming|sense: For the creative friend, the broken world comes together again in rings as good comes into being through evil and purposes out of chance.
ring:chain:01#0|sense: The wedding ring of recurrence is linked to passionate longing for beloved eternity.
ring:chain:02#2|sense: In the speech imagined by the animals, returning to the same life includes Zarathustra’s renewed proclamation of the overman to human beings.
two-paths:chain:01#2|verb: becomes the subject of a question about return
two-paths:chain:01#2|sense: Zarathustra asks whether the moment itself has not already been and whether we must not eternally return.
two-paths:chain:02#0|verb: become the subject of a question to the dwarf
two-paths:chain:02#0|sense: Zarathustra asks the dwarf whether the two roads will contradict each other forever.
two-paths:chain:02#2|verb: is challenged before the question of return
two-paths:chain:02#2|sense: Zarathustra rejects the ease of the answer about the circle and asks whether they must not eternally return.
wheel:link:01:child|sense: The child is called both a wheel rolling out of itself and a first movement.
wheel:link:04:becoming|verb: is compared with the year of existence
wheel:link:04:becoming|sense: The animals place the eternal turning of the wheel of existence alongside the dying and renewed flowering of all things in the eternal year of existence.
wheel:link:05:agency|verb: does not connect thought, deed and image by a ground
wheel:link:05:agency|sense: The wheel of cause does not roll between the thought, the deed and the image of the deed; this denies a connection rather than assigning the wheel an active role in distinguishing them.
wheel:chain:01#2|sense: A sacred saying of yes is needed for the play of creation.
wheel:chain:02#2|verb: is linked to a renewed proclamation
wheel:chain:02#2|sense: In the speech imagined by the animals, returning to the same life includes Zarathustra’s renewed word about the great noon of earth and humanity.
will-to-power:link:05:becoming|verb: threatens values in the stream of becoming
will-to-power:link:05:becoming|sense: The wisest place their values on the stream of becoming; the danger to these values is the will to power itself, life’s inexhaustible generative will.
will-to-power:link:06:will|verb: raises the question of willing backwards
will-to-power:link:06:will|sense: The will to power must will more than reconciliation with time; how it can will backwards remains a question.
will-to-power:chain:01#2|verb: requires the destruction of former values
will-to-power:chain:01#2|sense: Whoever must create good and evil must first destroy values; good and evil themselves overcome themselves again and again.
will-to-power:chain:02#1|verb: sets the task of going beyond reconciliation
will-to-power:chain:02#1|sense: The will to power must will more than reconciliation with time; its own deliverance and how it can will backwards remain questions.
will-to-power:chain:02#2|verb: raises the question of liberation from revenge
will-to-power:chain:02#2|sense: The will’s own deliverance is linked to the question whether it has unlearned the spirit of revenge.
will:link:02:body-self|sense: The creating body makes spirit an instrument of its own will; the creating Self is linked to valuation, pleasure and pain.
will:link:04:revenge|verb: takes revenge on the suffering out of powerlessness before the past
will:link:04:revenge|sense: The will cannot will backwards; its aversion to time and what has come to pass finds expression in revenge against all that can suffer.
will:link:05:redemption|verb: seeks liberation from the spirit of revenge
will:link:05:redemption|sense: The captive will is given the task of becoming its own deliverer and unlearning revenge against time; Zarathustra asks whether this has been achieved.
will:link:07:necessity|sense: Zarathustra addresses his will as his necessity and the reversal of all need and asks it to guard him against small victories.
will:chain:01#0|verb: takes revenge out of powerlessness before the past
will:chain:01#0|sense: Unable to will backwards, the will takes revenge on all that can suffer; revenge itself is its aversion to time and “it was”.
will:chain:01#2|verb: seeks to will the past creatively
will:chain:01#2|sense: Deliverance is conceived as the creative transformation of “it was” into “thus I willed it”; whether it is accomplished remains a question.
will:chain:02#2|sense: The play of creation requires sacred affirmation; the spirit wills its own will, and the one who has lost the world wins their own world.
animals--zarathustra--1|sense: The animals do not leave the sick Zarathustra; the eagle brings food, though Zarathustra does not eat for a long time.
animals--wisdom--7|verb: are compared with the image of wisdom
animals--wisdom--7|sense: Pride and intelligence are associated with the eagle and the snake; the female figure of wisdom in another scene introduces a dispute about life. Their resemblance does not make them one character.
animals-eagle#0|sense: The eagle and the snake appear in the sky; Zarathustra says they have gone to find out whether he is alive.
beggar--bestowing-virtue--2|sense: After the poor people’s rejection, Zarathustra tells the beggar that giving well is harder than receiving well; the text does not show that the beggar has mastered this art.
beggar--animals--4|verb: receives an invitation to the animals
beggar--animals--4|sense: Zarathustra invites the beggar to spend the night with the animals, talk with them about happiness and eat honey.
beggar-gift#2|verb: receives an invitation to the animals
beggar-gift#2|sense: Zarathustra offers him the chance to go to the eagle and the snake and talk with them about happiness.
beggar-gift#3|verb: receives permission to keep his custom
beggar-gift#3|sense: Zarathustra lets him keep to his own food, provided it makes him cheerful.
child-mirror--disciples--2|verb: prompts a search for lost friends
child-mirror--disciples--2|sense: The dream leads to the decision to seek lost friends; the text here calls them friends without identifying all of them as disciples.
child-mirror--child--4|verb: is compared with the child of a new beginning
child-mirror--child--4|sense: The image of a child appears in different scenes: the creative beginning in I.02 and the disturbing mirror of the teaching in II.01; the images are not asserted to be identical.
daughters--lion--3|verb: become the audience for a moral roar
daughters--lion--3|sense: The singer ironically portrays a European moral lion before the girls; their actions are not named as the cause of the roar.
daughters--memory--5|verb: are compared with the search for home
daughters--memory--5|sense: The memory of a pleasant oasis can be compared with the shadow’s homelessness, but the text does not claim that the girls became his home.
daughters-song#2|verb: become the audience for a moral roar
daughters-song#2|sense: The singer portrays a moral lion before the girls and ironically links its howling to European virtue.
daughters-song#3|verb: ends the song with a refrain
daughters-song#3|sense: The shadow repeats the line about the growing desert.
disciples--hunchback--5|verb: become the audience for a different speech
disciples--hunchback--5|sense: The hunchback hears the conversation and notices the difference between Zarathustra’s words to him, to the disciples and to himself; the disciples are not shown deliberately letting him hear it.
disciples--sailors--6|verb: want to tell of the sailors
disciples--sailors--6|sense: The disciples are so eager to tell of the sailors and the flying man that they scarcely listen to Zarathustra.
disciples-freedom#1|verb: are told to leave and find themselves
disciples-freedom#1|sense: The teacher demands departure and an independent search, rather than merely permitting them to leave.
disciples-freedom#3|sense: One beloved disciple offers an interpretation of the dream through Zarathustra’s life; whether that interpretation is accepted remains open.
dwarf--recurrence--4|verb: hears the question of the moment’s return after his answer about the circle
dwarf--recurrence--4|sense: In the dispute over the two paths, Zarathustra rejects the dwarf’s hasty formula and asks whether the moment itself returns with all the things connected to it.
dwarf--courage--5|verb: meets the challenge of Zarathustra’s courage
dwarf--courage--5|sense: Under the dwarf’s pressure, Zarathustra draws on his courage and says to him: “You! Or I!”
dwarf--dance--6|verb: becomes an image of what one dances over
dwarf--dance--6|sense: In Zarathustra’s question, heavy dwarfs and moles are needed for the lightest as things through and over which to dance.
dwarf-weight#2|verb: also conceals what is one’s own and burdens one with others’ values
dwarf-weight#2|sense: In another speech, the same named spirit obstructs the discovery of what is one’s own and is linked to the heavy words and values of others that a person carries on their shoulders.
fire-dog--will-to-power--3|verb: shows envy comparable to the struggle for power
fire-dog--will-to-power--3|sense: The dog is jealous of the state’s claim to be the most important beast; his reaction can be read alongside the speech on the will to power, while preserving the difference between scene and interpretation.
fire-dog-depth#0|verb: asks about the church and hears an answer about the state
fire-dog-depth#0|sense: The dog interrupts Zarathustra with a question about the church; Zarathustra calls it the most mendacious kind of state.
fool--zarathustra--1|sense: The people call the fool Zarathustra’s ape because he has adopted his turns of phrase and borrows from his wisdom.
fool--agency--3|verb: blocks the way and is told to pass by
fool--agency--3|sense: The fool stops Zarathustra at the gate and demands that he turn back; Zarathustra advises passing by where one can no longer love, and himself passes by the fool and the city.
fool-passing#0|verb: blocks the way and urges him to turn back
fool-passing#0|sense: The fool stands before Zarathustra at the gate and persuades him not to enter the city.
fool-passing#1|sense: Zarathustra names revenge for a lack of flattery as the motive for the fool’s speech.
fool-passing#3|verb: is passed by along with the city
fool-passing#3|sense: The narrator ends the scene with Zarathustra passing by both.
god--saint--1|verb: is the object of the saint’s love and praise
god--saint--1|sense: The saint says he loves God instead of human beings and praises his God by singing, weeping, laughing and grumbling.
god--ass--4|verb: is declared returned in the worship of the ass
god--ass--4|sense: The shadow explains the ass cult by saying that the ugliest man resurrected the old God; the pope prefers to worship God in this form rather than in none.
god--overman--5|verb: gives way to the wish that the overman live
god--overman--5|sense: After the death of God, Zarathustra calls on the higher men to wish for the overman to live and sees an open future for humanity.
god-loss#4|verb: is declared resurrected in the ass cult
god-loss#4|sense: The participants in the ass festival worship the ass; the shadow links this to the resurrection of the old God.
higher-men--zarathustra--1|verb: are found by Zarathustra to be the source of a many-voiced cry
higher-men--zarathustra--1|sense: Zarathustra finds the guests in his cave and learns that their voices together make up the cry for help he heard.
higher-men--overman--2|verb: hear the call to will that the overman live
higher-men--overman--2|sense: After the death of God, Zarathustra calls on the higher men to will that the overman live and explains his own hope for humanity as a crossing over.
higher-men--laughter--3|verb: are called to learn to laugh at themselves
higher-men--laughter--3|sense: Zarathustra calls their inability to dance beyond themselves a shortcoming, throws them the crown of the laughing one and calls on them to learn laughter.
higher-men--affirmation--6|verb: recognize a change when asked about repeating life
higher-men--affirmation--6|sense: The ugliest man’s question whether the others want to say “once more” to life makes the higher men aware of their transformation and recovery.
higher-men-recovery#1|verb: are called to learn to laugh
higher-men-recovery#1|sense: Zarathustra throws the higher men a crown and calls on them to learn to laugh.
hunchback--zarathustra--1|verb: tests the teaching with a request for healing and a question to the teacher
hunchback--zarathustra--1|sense: Speaking for the cripples, the hunchback proposes healing as a way to persuade them and then asks Zarathustra about the difference between his words to different listeners and to himself.
hunchback--will--3|verb: listens to the speech about the captive will addressed to the disciples
hunchback--will--3|sense: After answering the hunchback, Zarathustra speaks to the disciples about the will’s powerlessness before the past; the hunchback listens and later asks about the difference between his addresses.
jester--zarathustra--2|verb: demands that he leave, threatening to leap
jester--zarathustra--2|sense: The jester orders Zarathustra to leave the town; otherwise he promises to leap over him tomorrow, a living man over a dead one.
jester--fate--3|sense: Zarathustra reflects that the jester may become the fate of human existence deprived of meaning.
jester-leap#2|verb: threatens another leap if he refuses to leave
jester-leap#2|sense: The jester demands that Zarathustra leave the town, otherwise promising to leap over him the next day.
jester-overleaping#2|verb: places beside it an objection from the new tablet
jester-overleaping#2|sense: Later Zarathustra opposes the jester’s idea of leaping over the human being with many ways of overcoming; how this objection relates to his own promise remains a matter of comparison.
kings-rank#3|verb: offer the wine they brought for the meal
kings-rank#3|sense: The king on the left tells the guests about the wine he and his brother have stocked and brought on the ass.
last-pope--zarathustra--3|sense: The pope suggests that piety leads Zarathustra to unbelief, predicts that his honesty will lead him beyond good and evil, and senses a blessing in his presence.
last-pope--fate--5|verb: hears Zarathustra’s preference to make his own fate
last-pope--fate--5|sense: In conversation with the pope, Zarathustra rejects such a God and prefers to make his own fate, even to be a fool or to be God himself.
pope-worship#3|verb: later worships the ass as an image of God
pope-worship#3|sense: In the cave the pope joins in worshipping the ass and rejoices that he again has something to worship; its connection to his earlier request for shelter remains a sequence of scenes.
laughing-lion--wisdom--7|sense: The final lion’s gentle roaring recalls Zarathustra’s wish that his wild lioness-wisdom learn to roar gently for his friends.
lion-sign#1|verb: caresses Zarathustra and laughs with the doves
lion-sign#1|sense: The lion presses against Zarathustra and licks away his tears; the doves caress Zarathustra, and their flight above the lion’s nose makes him laugh.
life--zarathustra--4|sense: Life says that Zarathustra intends to leave her; after his undisclosed whisper they weep together.
life-love#2|verb: speaks of the intention to leave
life-love#2|sense: Life reproaches Zarathustra and says that he is thinking of leaving her soon.
life-love#3|sense: After the whisper and their shared weeping, Life is dearer to Zarathustra than his wisdom has ever been.
magician--shadow--6|sense: The shadow takes the magician’s harp and begins his song of the daughters of the desert.
pale-criminal--overman--4|verb: becomes the occasion for directing the judges toward the overman
pale-criminal--overman--4|sense: In the face of the pale criminal’s execution, Zarathustra demands compassion rather than revenge from the judges and love of the overman as a justification for their own continuing lives.
pale-criminal--fate--5|verb: is compared with the will before the past
pale-criminal--fate--5|sense: The criminal’s captivity to the image of one deed can be compared with the will’s inability to change “it was”; these are different problems, and the book does not call the first a cause or a particular case of the second.
criminal-image#0|verb: suggests robbery or revenge in addition to blood
criminal-image#0|sense: Failing to understand the thirst for blood, poor reason persuades the criminal at least to rob or take revenge; this suggestion does not make robbery the original motive for the murder.
criminal-image#3|sense: Reason’s paralysis under the weight of guilt and self-condemnation describe the same criminal, but the text does not derive the latter from the former.
people--tightrope-walker--2|verb: one of the people demands to see the tightrope walker
people--tightrope-walker--2|sense: One listener’s shout becomes the signal for the tightrope walker, who takes the words as addressed to him.
people--creation--4|sense: Zarathustra refuses to speak to the people as a herd and seeks living companions who create new values independently and together.
people-audience#0|verb: ask for the last man instead of the overman
people-audience#0|sense: The crowd wants to become last men and offers Zarathustra the overman.
people-audience#2|verb: gives way to the search for living co-creators
people-audience#2|sense: After the marketplace scene, Zarathustra decides to speak to companions rather than the people and seeks those who write new values.
sailors--dwarf--2|verb: listen to an account of the dispute with the dwarf
sailors--dwarf--2|sense: Zarathustra addresses his vision to the sailors; in it he asks the dwarf about time and rejects the lightness of his answer.
sailors--fire-dog--5|verb: precede the fire-dog story with an account of a figure they saw
sailors--fire-dog--5|sense: The sailors near the fire island report a vision around which a rumor arises; the narrative then introduces Zarathustra’s conversation with the fire dog.
shadow--daughters--3|verb: recalls clear air among the daughters of the desert
shadow--daughters--3|sense: The shadow compares the clear air of the cave with the bright air he once knew among the girls and performs a song composed for them.
shadow--ass--5|verb: explains the worship of the ass by God’s return
shadow--ass--5|sense: The shadow takes part in the worship of the ass and claims that the ugliest man resurrected the old God.
shadow--creation--7|verb: shows the danger of freedom without a goal
shadow--creation--7|sense: The shadow’s loss of a goal gives concrete form to the question of what the creator is free for; Zarathustra fears that a rigid faith will take hold of him.
shadow-home#2|verb: sings of the daughters of the desert
shadow-home#2|sense: In Zarathustra’s cave, the shadow recalls the bright air among the girls and sings a song composed there.
shadow-home#3|sense: The shadow explains his participation in the ass festival by claiming that the old God is alive again and attributes his resurrection to the ugliest man.
shepherd--recurrence--5|verb: echoes in Zarathustra’s illness and deliverance
shepherd--recurrence--5|sense: The shepherd’s bite echoes Zarathustra’s own bite; Zarathustra links his choking to disgust at the eternal return of the small human being.
shepherd--zarathustra--6|sense: The vision of the shepherd allows Zarathustra to be recognized in him through the repeated biting and spitting out, but does not establish their identity or the teacher’s final transformation.
shepherd-transformation#1|sense: After failing to pull the snake out, Zarathustra cries to the shepherd to bite off its head.
soothsayer--recurrence--3|verb: touches on the horror of return in his words
soothsayer--recurrence--3|sense: The soothsayer’s words render knowledge meaningless alongside Zarathustra’s sorrow over the eternal return of the small human being.
soothsayer--kings--6|verb: prompts the king’s answer about the supply of wine
soothsayer--kings--6|sense: In response to the soothsayer’s request, the king on the left says that both kings have brought enough wine in advance.
soothsayer--creation--8|verb: tempts with compassion before the choice of work
soothsayer--creation--8|sense: Zarathustra recalls the soothsayer’s temptation to compassion and turns to his work; the connection of this work to creation can be read through II.02.
tarantulas--difference--2|verb: swear revenge on all who are unlike them
tarantulas--difference--2|sense: In the oath Zarathustra attributes to them, the tarantulas threaten revenge and shame on all who are unlike them.
tarantula-revenge#1|sense: Zarathustra refuses to be confused with the preachers of equality and says that human beings are not equal.
tightrope-walker--jester--1|sense: Seeing his rival leap over him, the tightrope walker loses his head and his footing and falls.
walker-companion#2|verb: is carried and sheltered after death
walker-companion#2|sense: Zarathustra takes the tightrope walker’s body on his back and then leaves it in a hollow tree, protecting it from wolves.
walker-companion#3|verb: is called the first companion at parting
walker-companion#3|sense: Zarathustra addresses the buried man as his first companion and parts from him before seeking living co-creators.
ugliest-affirmation#2|verb: receives an offer of shelter and another path
ugliest-affirmation#2|sense: Zarathustra offers the self-exile his cave and conversation with the animals; the invitation does not yet show that he accepts.
wisdom--lion--3|verb: is portrayed as a lioness wished to roar gently
wisdom--lion--3|sense: Zarathustra fears that wild wisdom will frighten his friends and wishes his lioness-wisdom to learn to roar gently.
wisdom--child--4|verb: is compared with the child of creation through the image of birth
wisdom--child--4|sense: Wisdom’s birth of something new echoes the child as a new beginning of creation; this compares two images without identifying the offspring with the spirit’s final transformation.
wisdom--affirmation--6|verb: wishes every day to be holy
wisdom--affirmation--6|sense: The wisdom of youth once said that all days should be sacred; in the funeral song this sounds as a memory of lost joy.
wisdom-abundance#2|verb: disputes the reason for praising life
wisdom-abundance#2|sense: Wild wisdom claims that Zarathustra praises life out of desire and love; her statement remains part of a tense conversation.
wisdom-abundance#3|verb: arouses Life’s jealousy and is linked to her love
wisdom-abundance#3|sense: Life is jealous of Zarathustra’s wisdom and connects the endurance of her love with wisdom’s not leaving.
youth--creation--3|verb: hears of the noble one’s creation
youth--creation--3|sense: Zarathustra counts the youth among the noble and distinguishes the noble one’s striving to create a new virtue from the good person’s striving to preserve the old.
youth--courage--4|verb: is compared with the courage of warriors
youth--courage--4|sense: The call to the youth to preserve the hero and hope can be compared with the speech to warriors about courage and the highest hope; the book does not say that the youth has learned courage.
zarathustra--soothsayer--4|verb: objects to the soothsayer and invites him to joy
zarathustra--soothsayer--4|sense: Zarathustra is struck by the prophetic sadness; later he affirms that the blessed isles still exist and invites the soothsayer to share the evening’s joy.
zarathustra--wisdom--10|sense: Wild wisdom gives birth to her child on lonely mountains and seeks a place to lay it: on the tender grass of friends’ hearts.
zarathustra--recurrence--15|verb: experiences disgust at the return of the small human being
zarathustra--recurrence--15|sense: The thought of the eternal return of even the smallest human being becomes a disgust with all existence and an illness that Zarathustra tells the animals about.
zarathustra--zarathustra-soul--18|sense: The overflowing soul does not want to weep; Zarathustra predicts that it will then have to sing, and at the end asks it to sing.
